topics.title: Tonal vs. atonal music
topics.summary: Tonal music is organised around a tonal centre: a seven-note stepwise scale gives a key (tonic + mode, e.g. C major). Atonal music has no such centre.

terms.def: the central pitch of a key

topics.title: Notation: staff, clefs, notes, rests, accidentals
topics.summary: The grand staff joins a treble and a bass staff with a brace; middle C = C4. Key signature, time signature, bar lines, measures and ledger lines organise the page.
rules: An accidental applies only to the pitch it is written on (same line/space and octave) until the bar line.
Stems on notes go up on the right of the note head, down on the left; flags always point to the right.
guidelines: A dot adds half of the note value (× 1½).
A tie adds durations of the same pitch; a slur groups different pitches (articulation) — do not confuse them.

topics.title: Half steps and whole steps
topics.summary: A half step (semitone, m2) and a whole step (M2) are the building blocks of scales. A diatonic half step changes letter (D–E♭); a chromatic half step keeps the letter (D–D♯) and works as "colour".

terms.def: same letter name, e.g. D–D♯; decorative

guidelines: Half steps act as melodic intensifiers: they pull toward their goal more strongly than whole steps.

topics.title: The major scale, solfège and scale-degree names
topics.summary: A diatonic (heptatonic) scale has 5 whole and 2 half steps. Major: W W H W W W H.
guidelines: Fixed-do solfège names pitches (do = C always); movable-do names scale degrees (do = the tonic). Know which system your class uses.

topics.title: Minor scales: natural, harmonic, melodic
topics.summary: Natural minor: W H W W H W W (7̂ is the subtonic, a whole step below the tonic). Harmonic minor raises 7̂ to make a leading tone (gap of 1½ steps between 6̂ and 7̂). Melodic minor raises 6̂ and 7̂ going up and returns to natural minor coming down.
rules: In minor, raise 7̂ whenever it acts as a leading tone (e.g. in V and vii°).
guidelines: Use raised 6̂ when ascending 6̂–7̂–8̂ to avoid the augmented 2nd; use natural 6̂ and 7̂ when descending 8̂–7̂–6̂.

topics.title: Chromatic scale, enharmonics, chromatic passing tones
topics.summary: The chromatic (12-tone) scale moves by 12 half steps. By convention it is spelled with sharps going up and flats going down. Enharmonic notes sound the same but are spelled differently (A♯/B♭).
rules: Ascending chromatic scale: use sharps; descending: use flats.
guidelines: In a chromatic passing motion (F–F♯–G) the chromatic step usually comes first, then the diatonic step.

topics.title: Modes and their characteristic notes
topics.summary: Each diatonic mode starts on a different degree of the major scale. Compare each mode with Ionian (for the major-3rd modes) or Aeolian (for the minor-3rd modes); the interval that differs is its characteristic note. Ordered by their 3rd and by the number of flats relative to Ionian, the modes run from brightest (Lydian) to darkest (Locrian).
rules: The characteristic note cannot be the root (tonic) of the mode.
guidelines: Scale → mode → intervals: all diatonic intervals appear in the modes (P1, m2, M2, m3, M3, P4, A4/d5 (tritone), P5, m6, M6, m7, M7, P8).

topics.title: Keys and the circle of fifths
topics.summary: Going clockwise by perfect fifths adds a sharp; going counter-clockwise adds a flat. Each major key shares its signature with the relative minor a minor 3rd below.

topics.title: Interval size + quality
topics.summary: An interval has a size (count the letter names: unison, 2nd … octave) and a quality (perfect, major, minor, augmented, diminished). Even sizes go line→space; odd sizes go line→line or space→space.
rules: Group 1 (unison, 4th, 5th, octave): d ← P → A.
Group 2 (2nd, 3rd, 6th, 7th): d ← m ← M → A.
guidelines: Vertical (harmonic) intervals sound together; horizontal (melodic) intervals sound in succession.
Quick method: compare the upper note with the major scale of the lower note.

topics.title: Compound intervals and inversion
topics.summary: A compound interval is larger than an octave; subtract 7 to find its simple form (m9 → m2). Inverting an interval moves the lower note up an octave.
rules: Inversion: the sizes add up to 9 (3rd ↔ 6th, 4th ↔ 5th, 2nd ↔ 7th).
Inversion: M ↔ m, A ↔ d, P ↔ P.

topics.title: The overtone series
topics.summary: A sounding tone contains a fundamental plus overtones at whole-number frequency ratios. The overtones give each instrument its timbre (tone colour); real instruments show slight inharmonicity.
guidelines: The major triad (M3 + P5 above the root) is the most stable chord because it appears in the series (partials 4:5:6).
Perfect fifths are especially significant; the stable intervals are P8, P5, M3, m3 (M3 more than m3).
The P4 above the bass does not arise from the fundamental the way P5 does; it is the less stable inversion of P5.

topics.title: Consonance, dissonance and stability
topics.summary: Consonant intervals are perfect (P1, P5, P8) or imperfect (3rds, 6ths). Dissonant intervals are 2nds, 7ths and all augmented and diminished intervals. The P4 depends on context.
rules: A P4 above the bass is dissonant (tension: it moves to 3̂, e.g. F over C → E over C); a P4 between upper voices, as the inversion of a P5, is consonant (relaxation).

topics.title: Key-defining progressions (tritone and leading tone)
topics.summary: Dissonant intervals built on the leading tone point to one key. The tritone resolves inward or outward; the d7/A2 pair comes from the leading tone and ♭6̂ in minor.
rules: d5 → M3 (contracts); its inversion A4 → m6 (expands).
d7 → P5; its inversion A2 → P4 (a consonant P4, inversion of P5).
Chromatic resolutions: M6 → A6 → P8 (expands) and its inversion m3 → d3 → P1.

topics.title: Rhythm, beat and tempo
topics.summary: Rhythm combines duration, pitch, accent and silence. The beat is a steady, recurring pulse; tempo is the speed of the beat. Assign a number of beats to a note value (if 𝅝 = 4, then 𝅗𝅥 = 2 and ♩ = 1).

topics.title: Meter and time signatures
topics.summary: Meter is a sense of regular beats with regular subdivision. Simple meters divide the beat in two; compound meters divide it in three. Duple, triple and quadruple count the beats per bar.
rules: Simple meter: top number = beats per bar (2, 3, 4); bottom number = beat note (4 = quarter).
Compound meter: top number = divisions per bar (6, 9, 12); bottom = division note; three divisions make one dotted beat.

topics.title: Tuplets, syncopation, harmonic rhythm, hemiola
topics.summary: Tuplets borrow a division from the other meter type (triplets in simple meter, duplets in compound). Syncopation places accents where the meter would not put them. Harmonic rhythm is how often the chords change.
guidelines: Harmonic rhythm shapes the emotional effect of a passage.
A hemiola regroups two bars of triple meter as three bars of duple (common before Baroque cadences).

topics.title: Harmonic progression chart (circle of fifths)
topics.summary: Chords normally move toward the tonic through the circle of fifths: iii → vi → IV/ii → V/vii° → I in major; VII → III → VI → iv/ii° → V/vii° → i in minor. IV and ii (subdominant group) can go to each other (IV → ii), and V can go to vii°. Arrows that skip ahead are allowed; backward motion breaks the flow.

tables.title: Flow chart (notes p.14)
rows: iii → vi → [IV → ii] → [V ↔ vii°] → I  (any chord can go to the right; I can go anywhere)
VII → III → VI → [iv → ii°] → [V ↔ vii°] → i

topics.title: Harmonizing a melody: 5-step procedure
topics.summary: A routine for choosing chords under a given melody.
rules: 1. Start and end with I (if possible).
2. Make the penultimate chord V (if possible).
3. Write all chord options under each melody note.
4. Check the harmonic progression against the flow chart.
5. Avoid repetition: change the chord for every melody note.

topics.title: Figured bass and inversion figures
topics.summary: Figures give intervals above the bass. Only the bass is fixed; the upper voices are free to be arranged.
rules: An accidental alone (♯, ♭, ♮) applies to the 3rd above the bass.
A slash through a figure (4̸, 6̸, 5̸) raises that note a half step.
Only the bass note is fixed; upper voices may be voiced freely.
